issues.legal_issue: Land may be ancestral when its possession is recorded in the hands of a remote direct ancestor, even though possession by the immediate common ancestor is not recorded, if the land’s history indicates no acquisition other than inheritance.
material_facts: Revenue records traced some of the disputed land to the possession of a remote direct ancestor.
The claimants traced their descent through the family line from that ancestor.
Although the immediate common ancestor’s possession was not shown in the revenue records, the history of the land gave no indication that it had been acquired other than by inheritance.
issues.conclusion: The land traced to the remote direct ancestor was ancestral, and the lower appellate court was right to treat that portion as ancestral.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, ancestral character depends on descent from a lineal ancestor through whom the claimants also claim; proof that the immediate common ancestor possessed the land is not indispensable where possession by a more remote direct ancestor is shown and the land’s history indicates acquisition only by inheritance. The Court distinguished the principle in Attar Singh v. Thakar Singh (1908) and approved Haveldar Mihan Singh v. Piara Singh (1946) and Gurdev Singh v. Dasa(u)ndhi (AIR 1948 EP 22). No statutory provision was relied on.

issues.legal_issue: When ancestral and non-ancestral land is replaced by a consolidated area, the part of the replacement area corresponding to the ancestral land retains its ancestral character.
material_facts: The disputed land had fallen to the testator’s share in consolidation proceedings in lieu of land held by him.
The land given in lieu included both ancestral and non-ancestral land.
The ancestral component could be identified by tracing the relevant land records and determining the corresponding area.
issues.conclusion: The portion of the consolidated area corresponding to the ancestral land was ancestral.
issues.legal_principle: A consolidated replacement area does not lose the ancestral character of the part corresponding to the ancestral land exchanged for it. The Court relied on Haveldar Mihan Singh v. Piara Singh (1946) and Gurdev Singh v. Dasa(u)ndhi (AIR 1948 EP 22), which recognize apportionment of consolidated land according to the areas of ancestral and non-ancestral land. No statutory provision was relied on.
